articles.title: Canoe Tripping at Kanawana

status_history.note: Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 113 (Vol. 29 No. 3, May 1977): new subsection 'November 1975: every paddler in a lifejacket, by federal law' -- the Small Vessels Regulations amendment that ended the canoe and rowboat exemption, Jocelyn Palm's CCA survey (nearly half of camps already required flotation; 18% did not learn of the regulation until they read it in this magazine and a further 10% not until the questionnaire arrived), and her recommended waterfront syllabus. Gives a hard date for flotation equipment on every La Verendrye trip from summer 1976. Source 13.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 122 (Vol. 30 No. 6, December 1978): new subsection on the association's editorial about a fatal wilderness canoe trip in Quebec in 1978 -- unnamed in the source and not identified here -- and its judgement that a decade of confidence in Canadian camp tripping standards had been misplaced, plus the 1920s Balsam Lake precedent credited with producing the 'hang on to the canoe' rule and standard strokes. Source 14; feeds new priority p_322.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 131 (Vol. 32 No. 3, May 1980): new section 'What the movement decided, 1980' -- the free-text answers to question 139 of the Society of Camp Directors' tripping questionnaire, printed unattributed and disagreeing sharply about standards, certification and liability; and the Ontario Camping Association's emergency procedures with the reporting policy adopted effective February 1980. Stated there that this is Ontario policy and that no evidence of Quebec's equivalent appears here. Source 15.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 132 (Vol. 32 No. 4, June 1980): new section 'What a Canadian camp canoe trip looked like in 1980' -- Michael Hoyer's report of the Society of Camp Directors' survey of about sixty camps across eight provinces, with leader and camper ages and qualifications, staff-camper ratios, equipment rankings, hull types (two-thirds still canvas), trip sizes, and the finding that five years after the federal flotation regulation only about a third of camps required lifejackets to be worn. Also names trip logs and camper and staff trip evaluations as a further record class to seek. A national survey, not a Kanawana document. Source 16.

articles.title: The Canadian Camping Movement

status_history.note: Corrected the QCA/ACQ relationship: the article called the ACQ the QCA's 'modern successor'. Lazanik's announcement in Canadian Camping Vol. 21 No. 4 (Summer 1969) shows the ACQ was founded 1958, joined the QCA in 1961 as a parallel section under a Conseil Provincial, and merged into the CCA in 1969. Source [8s] added. Found by the full word-for-word read (kb/reread/cc_findings.md, issue 83).

Charles Plewman's 1971 account added (source 8t): a founder dating the CCA's formation to 1946 at the Chateau Laurier, Ottawa, with no corporate existence at that point and membership effectively Ontario and Quebec only. A second independent source for 1946, with a venue. Found by the full word-for-word read (kb/reread/cc_findings.md, issue 92).

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 109-110: new paragraph 'The government arrives alongside the association, 1976' -- the High Commission of Leisure and Sports funding a full-time provincial camp-training post inside the ACQ-QCA (October 1976), the Quebec Department of Labour's proposed six-foot limit on camp waterfront depth and the new Day Camp Standards Committee (December 1976), and the parallel pattern of government grants conditional on accreditation in New Brunswick, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Lettered sub-source 8z added; header count unchanged at 13.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 111 (Vol. 29 No. 1, February 1977): three new paragraphs -- the $300,000 Quebec provincial grant for the association's spring training programme and the province-wide 'Camp Week' of 5-11 March 1977 with Rosaire Corbin named as training officer; the English Section's 40th Anniversary Banquet of 26 March 1977, a fourth independent corroboration of the 1937 founding; and the amended Employment Visa Certification Waiver, which from 1977 let camps operated by CCA members hire foreign counsellors without a Canada Manpower labour-market test. Lettered sub-source 8aa added; header count unchanged at 13.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 112 (Vol. 29 No. 2, March 1977): new paragraph on the CCA's first annual statistical questionnaire -- 68,000 camper spaces, 260,000 campers, 32,000 staff (22,000 paid, 10,000 volunteer, 1,600 from outside Canada), $8m food and $14m other costs for 1976 -- with the editor's warning to non-responding directors that refusing the association's questions would invite government legislation instead. Sub-source 8ab; header count unchanged at 13.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 116: new paragraphs on how the CCA became a bilingual association -- Paul Belanger persuading the board at Regina in 1971, producing Le Comite des Camps Francais and a new constitution recognising both language groups -- with Belanger's record (Camp-Ecole Keno 1964, ACQ president, first president of the CCA French Language Camping Committee, chairman of the first French Language Camping Conference at Montmorency Forest in April 1976) and the structural consequence for Kanawana's own accrediting body. Sub-source 8ac; header count unchanged at 13.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 117: new paragraph recording that the QCA executive met monthly at the Montreal YMCA through 1978 -- the provincial body that accredited Kanawana, presided over by Kanawana's own director, meeting in the building of the institution that owned the camp -- together with the section's public programme for the year. Sub-source 8ad; header count unchanged at 13.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 119: extended the foreign-counsellor paragraph with the 1978 change -- the revised Immigration Act of 10 April 1978, the Ministry of Employment and Immigration's letter to the CCA president retaining the Manpower Certification exemption for the 1978 season only 'with the change likely coming this fall', and the new pre-arrival employment authorization procedure (Form Imm. 1102, a camp letter establishing CCA membership in good standing, and a social insurance number). The exemption was therefore a narrow two-season window. Sub-source 8ae.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 122: three new paragraphs -- F. M. Van Wagner appointed President Emeritus, with the association stating he was a charter member of the 1936 founding and organised the QCA English Section the next year; the Quebec English Section's October 1978 panel on staff recruitment, training and supervision and the bilingual ACQ-QCA dinner meeting, with the Montreal people named; and Alan F. Klein's address to a CCA conference held in Montreal in 1960. Sub-source 8af; header count unchanged at 13.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 123 (Vol. 31 No. 1, February 1979): flagged a date discrepancy between the article's own sources -- source 8c gives the CCA's Letters Patent as 4 November 1949, the association's 1976 Directory Issue (8y) gives 5 November 1949. Not resolved; neither date treated as settled. Added the association's February 1979 self-description, 'It began in 1936 and became incorporated in 1949', as the day-free version, plus its statement of purposes, its automatic-membership rule and its dependence on Fitness and Amateur Sport funding. Sub-source 8ag.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 126: flagged a one-year discrepancy on Canada's first camp -- the article gives Big Cove as 1889 from an encyclopaedic entry, while CCA president Jack Pearse told the association's annual meeting in Nova Scotia on 25 May 1979 that organized children's camping in Canada 'began in Nova Scotia in 1890'. Recorded, not resolved; Kanawana's position as second-oldest is unaffected. Sub-source 8ah.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 128: recorded that the Quebec Camping Association English Section and the joint ACQ-QCA Provincial Board both drop out of the association's printed list of provincial associations between October 1978 and December 1979, leaving only the ACQ under Raymond Bonneau -- weak evidence, recorded as such, but consistent with the 'former English Section' of Walsh's 1983 award citation, and bracketing the change. Also recorded that the 1980 annual meeting moved from Quebec to Toronto. Sub-source 8ai.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 129 (Vol. 32 No. 1, February 1980): new section on the Quebec Camping Association's own Director Education Program, 'Formateurs-multiplicateurs', prepared February 1976 and serialised in the national newsletter -- recruitment sources including the association's own placement service, selection by interview on a standard ACQ form, guidance on interview setting and questions, and a self-assessment for the interviewer. The training Kanawana's directors were offered in the exact period of the camp's thinnest records. Sub-source 8aj.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 130 (Vol. 32 No. 2, March 1980): new section on the Ontario Camping Association's 'Suggested Camp Forms' kit -- nine standard forms named and priced, explicitly designed to be copied by any camp, covering every document class this read had been reconstructing piecemeal -- with the Camper's Health Certificate reproduced in full. Sub-source 8ak; feeds new priority p_323, which turns the list into an instruction to ask Concordia and Trent for Kanawana material by these exact names, and flags the embargo consequence.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 133: recorded the association's own statement that a camp is accredited only by its provincial association and is a member camp, not an accredited member, of the CCA -- fixing the form of words this project should use about Kanawana. Sub-source 8al.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 134: recorded that by 1980 the Association des Camps du Quebec set age and experience requirements for the camp director's post itself, from a Camp Amy Molson advertisement listing compliance as a condition of employment. Sub-source 8am.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 135 (Vol. 33 No. 1, February 1981): new section specifying what a camp staff manual contained -- site sketch with 'special problems which site gives rise to', a brief historical sketch of the camp, the role of camping in the sponsoring organization's programme, dismissal procedures and salary scales, sample forms including tripping reports and counsellor evaluations, and job analyses -- bound in a stiff loose-leaf cover with coloured section dividers. Makes a Kanawana staff manual a specific object to ask for, and retrospectively explains the already-held 1951 'Kamp Kanawana History' presented at a staff training course. Sub-source 8an; feeds p_323.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 137 (Vol. 33 No. 3, May 1981): new section on Robert E. Wilkinson's 'Camps, Their Planning and Management' (C.V. Mosby, 1981) -- the first comprehensive Canadian camp administration text, by a McGill physical education professor who was a CCA member through the Association des Camps du Quebec and associated with Camp Nominingue, containing specimens of every kind of camp business form and the CCA's national code of ethics. Also added the association's May 1981 memo that 'accredited by C.C.A.' is incorrect wording some camps were still using, with the consequence that any such Kanawana material should not be read as evidence of a second accreditation. Sub-source 8ao; feeds p_323.

status_history.note: Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 111: added a paragraph of context outside the embargo block, establishing that a director's written end-of-season assessment was recommended national practice -- John Latimer's February 1977 CCA promotion summary tells directors to send parents 'a letter of assessment from the Director' and to collect 'a full report from each counsellor'. Latimer is describing assessments of campers, not staff, and the article says so. Sources 5 -> 6.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 115: strengthened the context around the r_0001 embargo block with Barry Lowes's October 1977 account of end-of-season evaluation -- section heads evaluating all staff, mid-summer self-evaluations on the same form, and the director collating the reports into lists that include 'staff to be rehired'. Robitaille's rehire list is the last step of a nationally recommended procedure. Lowes also states the profession's standard of candour with confidentiality and the subject's right to see the report; the article notes that nothing shows whether the five named people were told. Sources 6 -> 7.

articles.title: The Order of the Knights of Kanawana
What the Plaques Say Besides Names

status_history.note: Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 111: added the CCA's own public-relations doctrine of February 1977 (John Latimer's talk to the OCA) as the antecedent to the promotion pamphlet Walsh's committee issued in 1981. Sources 6 -> 7.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 114 (Vol. 29 No. 4, June 1977): the QCA English Section presidency is a two-year term whose second year begins in June 1977 (so c. spring 1976 to spring 1978), and the section president is ex officio a Vice-President of the joint ACQ-QCA Provincial Board under Abbe Robert Maisonneuve. Two new table rows, including the March 1977 40th anniversary conference he presided over. Sources 7 -> 8.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 116 (Vol. 29 No. 6, December 1977): the association's own list of committee chairmen for 1977-78 names Walsh as chairman of the Public Relations Committee -- three years earlier than the article previously dated the chairmanship, and the only Quebec name among the eight committees. New table row; source 8 extended.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 121: the October 1978 provincial association contact list gives Dr. Ken R. Willis as QCA president, closing Walsh's two-year term at roughly spring 1976 - spring 1978. New table row; source 8 extended.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 124: the association's list of committee chairmen for 1978-79 again names Walsh as chairman of Public Relations and Promotion, so the table row now reads 1977-79 from two consecutive published slates, and he remains the only Quebec name among fifteen committees, projects and task forces. Source 8 extended.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 126 (Vol. 31 No. 4, June 1979): the CCA vice-presidency dated and placed -- installed at the annual meeting at Acadia University, Wolfville, on 25 May 1979, under President Clifford Labbett, for the 1979-81 term; the same meeting heard Ken Willis invite the association to meet in Quebec in spring 1980. Sources 8 -> 9.

Word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 128: CCA president Cliff Labbett independently confirms the two-year PR chairmanship ('a position he has held for the past two years'). Open Question 1 furnished on both sides -- the same issue confirms Camp Thunderbird as a real Victoria YM-YWCA camp of 1,300 acres, making a move between Y camps coherent, while Labbett describes Walsh entirely by his Quebec offices and says nothing of a move west. Question left open. Source 9 extended.
